questions.q: On a Hertzsprung-Russell diagram of luminosity against spectral class, where are the hot, luminous stars and which way does temperature run?
options: Hot stars are on the right and dim stars at the top; temperature increases to the right
Stars on the left side are hot and those on the right are cool, with the very luminous stars towards the top and the dim ones towards the bottom
Hot stars are at the bottom and cool stars at the top; luminosity increases to the left
All stars of the same temperature have the same luminosity, so the axes are interchangeable
questions.explanation: As the textbook states, on an H-R diagram stars on the left side are hot and those on the right are cool, while those towards the top are very luminous and those towards the bottom are dim. The most common exam trap is forgetting that the temperature axis runs backwards, hot on the left.

questions.q: On the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, why are giants and supergiants very bright despite their relatively cool, red surface temperature?
options: They are very close to Earth, so they appear brighter than they really are
They are fusing hydrogen far faster than main sequence stars of the same colour
They are very large stars, so even though their surface is cool they have such a large radiating surface that they are still very bright
Their cool surface temperature means each square metre radiates more energy than a hot star
questions.explanation: The textbook explains that giants and supergiants sit above the main sequence: many are red because of their cooler surface temperature, but are still very bright because they have such a large radiating surface. Luminosity depends on surface area as well as temperature, so at a fixed temperature the more luminous star must be the larger one.

questions.q: Below the main sequence on the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram is a cluster of hot, dim stars known as white dwarfs. What is true of a white dwarf?
options: It is made mainly of carbon, fusion has ceased in its core, and it is simply cooling down
It is fusing hydrogen rapidly in its core, which is why it is so hot
It is a very large, cool star swollen by heating in its outer layers
It is the most massive type of star and sits at the top left of the diagram
questions.explanation: The textbook describes white dwarfs as a cluster of hot, dim stars below the main sequence, made mainly of carbon, in which fusion has ceased in their cores so they are simply cooling down. They are hot but dim because they are tiny, roughly Earth-sized, with very little radiating surface.

questions.q: From memory: what do the main sequence stars on the diagonal band of the H-R diagram have in common, and how do the hotter, brighter stars differ from the cooler, dimmer ones?
keyPoints: Most stars cluster along a diagonal line from bright and hot down to dim and cool, the main sequence.
Main sequence stars are all doing much the same thing, fusing hydrogen in their cores, just like the Sun.
The hotter, brighter stars are more massive than the cooler, dimmer stars, and stars lie on the main sequence for most of their existence.
questions.explanation: If you recalled that the main sequence is the diagonal of hydrogen-fusing stars and that the hotter, brighter members are the more massive ones, grade yourself Good or Easy. Stars spend most of their lives on this band.

questions.q: In the first step of the proton-proton chain (PP1) in the Sun, two protons are forced together. What happens, since a nucleus of two protons alone is very unstable?
options: Both protons are destroyed, releasing two gamma rays and nothing else
One of the protons undergoes positive beta decay, releasing a positron, a neutrino and about 1.44 MeV, forming deuterium
The two protons immediately form a stable helium-4 nucleus
A neutron is captured from outside to make the pair stable
questions.explanation: The textbook gives this first PP1 step: two protons fuse, one undergoes positive beta decay releasing a positron, a neutrino and about 1.44 MeV, and the isotope formed is deuterium. The positron then annihilates with an electron and the neutrino streaks out of the Sun in seconds.

questions.q: When two hydrogen nuclei in the centre of a star fuse, 1.44 MeV of energy is released. How much mass is lost by the Sun in this reaction?
questions.explanation: This is the textbook's worked sample. First convert the energy to joules, then rearrange E = mc^2 to m = E/c^2. The mass lost per reaction is tiny, but the Sun holds on the order of 10^57 protons, so the cumulative output powers it for billions of years.

questions.q: The mass defect when a proton and a neutron combine to form a deuterium nucleus is 0.002388 u. Using 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c^2, calculate the binding energy of the deuterium nucleus.
questions.explanation: Rather than converting to kilograms and joules, the textbook uses the standard conversion 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c^2. Multiplying the mass defect of 0.002388 u by 931.5 gives the binding energy of deuterium, 2.224 MeV, the energy released when the proton and neutron combine.

questions.q: In the CNO cycle, what is the role of the carbon, nitrogen and oxygen, and how do its products compare with those of the proton-proton chain?
options: They are the fuel that is used up to make carbon; the CNO cycle produces carbon while the pp chain produces helium
They act as catalysts, present at the end with no net change in amount; the products are identical, both producing a helium-4 nucleus, 2 positrons, 2 neutrinos and gamma photons
They are waste products created only by the CNO cycle and not by the pp chain
They slow the reaction down, so the CNO cycle releases far less energy than the pp chain
questions.explanation: The textbook states that the carbon present at the start of the CNO cycle is present at the end, so there is no net change in its amount, and that carbon, nitrogen and oxygen are referred to as catalysts. It also confirms there is no difference in products: both routes produce a helium-4 nucleus, 2 positrons, 2 neutrinos and gamma photons.

questions.q: Compare the proton-proton chain and the CNO cycle as ways that stars fuse protons to form helium. (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: Both the proton-proton chain and the CNO cycle achieve the same net result: four protons are fused into one helium-4 nucleus, with identical products (a helium-4 nucleus, 2 positrons, 2 neutrinos and gamma photons), releasing energy. Whereas the proton-proton chain is the dominant process in lower-mass, cooler stars like the Sun and does not rely on any other nuclei, the CNO cycle features especially in stars more massive than the Sun where the core is hotter, and it relies on carbon, nitrogen and oxygen being present to act as catalysts. The difference is the pathway, the temperature required and the need for pre-existing carbon, not the products.

criteria.descriptor: States both fuse protons to helium-4 with the same net products.
Identifies the CNO cycle needs hotter, more massive stars and pre-existing carbon, the pp chain needs only protons.
Names carbon, nitrogen and oxygen as catalysts, consumed then regenerated with no net change.

questions.explanation: The textbook sample problem confirms there is no difference in products; both produce a helium-4 nucleus, 2 positrons, 2 neutrinos and 3 gamma photons. The marks come from the explicit contrast in pathway, temperature and the catalytic role of carbon.

questions.q: More massive stars than the Sun can fuse all the way to iron-56. Where do the elements heavier than iron come from?
options: They are also made by ordinary fusion in the cores of massive stars, just more slowly
They are made by rapid neutron capture, the r-process, in the conditions found during a supernova explosion at the end of a massive star's life
They were all made in the first few minutes of the big bang along with hydrogen and helium
They cannot be made at all, so iron-56 is the heaviest element in the universe
questions.explanation: The textbook notes that more massive stars can fuse to produce nuclei all the way to iron-56, but that nuclei heavier than iron are formed by the r-process, rapid neutron capture, in the abundance of free neutrons found during a supernova explosion. Iron-56 is the most stable nucleus, at the peak of the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve, so fusion cannot build past it.

questions.q: From memory, give the episode's three-tier 'Bang, Burn, Boom' summary of where the elements come from.
keyPoints: Bang: the big bang made hydrogen (~75%), helium (~25%) and a trace of lithium, and nothing heavier.
Burn: elements from carbon up to iron were forged by nuclear fusion in the cores of stars, but fusion can only build up to iron.
Boom: every element heavier than iron was made in the supernova explosion itself by rapid neutron capture, then scattered into space.
questions.explanation: If you recalled all three tiers and that fusion stops at iron because it sits at the peak of the binding-energy curve, grade yourself Good or Easy. The iron in your blood was made by fusion; the gold and uranium were made in a supernova.
